name: root vegetable skillet
instructions:
Everything raw in the oven — NEVER SAUTE. Root vegetables (carrots, celery root, turnips, radishes, red onions) tossed with olive oil, cinnamon, nutmeg, salt, and pepper, arranged in the skillet raw. Parsley scattered EARLY (goes in before the bake to get toasted). Sunflower seeds scattered on top. Cheese topping goes on partway through — split gruyere + parmesan (see notes on why not gruyere alone).

OPTIONAL — PARBOILED ROSEMARY POTATOES: parboil potatoes with rosemary until just-tender, then arrange them alongside the raw root vegetables. This is the parboiled-potato path — see notes.

BAKE TEMPERATURE:
- 375°F if NOT using parboiled potatoes (raw root vegetables only)
- 400°F WITH parboiled potatoes (higher heat needed to brown the already-tender potatoes)

Bake uncovered start to finish. Add the cheese topping partway through so it melts and browns rather than burns.
notes:
Red onions are not optional.

=== NEVER SAUTE — EVERYTHING RAW IN THE OVEN ===

The hard rule for this recipe: no stovetop sauté step. All root vegetables go into the skillet RAW and cook only in the oven. The only exception is parboiled potatoes if you're using them (see below). No pre-cooked onions, no sautéed carrots, no seared anything — the whole point is the oven-only, lidless bake as a single-step technique.

=== PARBOILED ROSEMARY POTATOES — OPTIONAL BUT NICE ===

You can squeeze in parboiled potatoes as an addition. Parboil them with rosemary (add rosemary sprigs or dried rosemary to the boiling water) so they pick up the rosemary flavor and start softening. Then arrange the parboiled potatoes alongside the raw root vegetables in the skillet. The rosemary + potato combination reads distinctly against the other roots and adds a starchy, herbal element the base recipe doesn't have.

WHY PARBOIL AND NOT RAW: raw potatoes take much longer to cook through than the other root vegetables. Adding them raw would either leave them undercooked or force overcooking the rest of the vegetables. Parboiling gets them to the same doneness stage as the raw roots by oven-start, so everything finishes together.

OVEN TEMP JUMP: with parboiled potatoes in the skillet, bump the oven from 375°F to 400°F. The higher heat is needed to brown the potatoes' already-tender surfaces (they won't caramelize at 375°F because they're not raw enough to develop maillard). Without parboiled potatoes, 375°F is right — the raw roots need the gentler heat.

=== CHEESE TOPPING — GRUYERE + PARMESAN SPLIT (NOT GRUYERE ALONE) ===

Split the cheese topping between gruyere and parmesan. Gruyere alone is a little too funky to carry the whole cheese layer — it adds a weird odor when it's the only cheese, especially against the earthy root vegetables. Parmesan alongside cuts the gruyere's funk with cleaner sharpness and grating-cheese umami.

Suggested split: maybe 60/40 or 50/50 gruyere-to-parmesan. Adjust to taste. Both cheeses grated and mixed before scattering on the skillet.

=== PARSLEY GOES IN EARLY — GETS TOASTED WITH THE POTATOES ===

Unusual for parsley in this cookbook: parsley goes in EARLY here, not as an off-heat finishing herb. Scatter it on the vegetables before baking so it toasts during the oven cook. Toasted parsley reads different from raw finishing parsley — more crisp/nutty than fresh/green. This is a common pairing with potatoes specifically (toasted-parsley-and-potato is a real combo). If you want a fresh green finish too, you can scatter a small extra handful of fresh parsley after the bake, but the load-bearing parsley move here is the toasted version.

=== FAILED EXPERIMENTS — APPLES + BUTTER (BOTH REMOVED, NOW CLASHING) ===

GREEN APPLES: tried adding green apples (granny smith) to the skillet. Didn't work — apples in an oven-baked root-vegetable skillet don't hold up the way they do in other formats. Removed and moved to clashing.

BUTTER: tried the butter + olive oil combo (butter for flavor, oil for volume — a pattern that works elsewhere in the cookbook, e.g. marcella-frittata). Doesn't work here. The recipe stays cleaner with olive oil alone. Butter removed and moved to clashing. Combined with the gruyere leaking its own fat (see FAILURE MODE below), adding butter overloaded the finished skillet.

=== FAILURE MODE — TOO MUCH OIL ===

Watch the total amount of olive oil. The gruyere leaks its own fat as it melts, so the finished skillet ends up with more fat than the oil-you-added-during-prep math suggests. Start conservative — you can always drizzle more later, but there's no fix for a greasy skillet.

=== SKIP THE ONION SAUTE — NOT NEEDED ===

Already covered by the NEVER SAUTE rule above, but worth restating: red onions go in raw. They soften enough during the oven cook. No pre-sauté saves a step and a pan.

=== COVERED VS UNCOVERED BAKE — LIDLESS IS THE MOVE ===

Covered attempts have all gone soggy, and no amount of post-uncover baking recovers the mush. Bake uncovered start to finish. Different from italian-tomato-white-beans (which wants a covered stage because it has a liquid bean base to steam the eggplant tian on top); here there's no liquid base and covering just traps vegetable moisture without a positive purpose.
why_i_like_this_recipe: It's a really unique way to use carrots — eat them baked/whole with spices and cheese (normally carrots are just sautee fodder). Also a great reason to buy celery root. And an excuse to buy gruyere cheese (with a parmesan chaser).
